quote: We so we were with Fluent Solar, but another business.
stewart_read: Customer names the prior installer (Fluent Solar) unprompted. This is exactly the kind of orphaned-system disclosure the schema's orphaned_flow branch is built for ('What company did you go with originally?'), but the rep doesn't probe further — no question about system size, ownership structure, or why they're moving off Fluent Solar before pivoting to the wife/co-owner question.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have judged this detail irrelevant since the customer already confirmed independent ownership, deprioritizing the probe to move faster through verify.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to always follow a named-competitor disclosure with at least one orphaned_flow question (ownership type, system size) — this is free competitive intel for whoever picks up the account next, and it also would have surfaced the removal/reinstall need earlier and more clearly.

quote: Is there any way on the title but you and your wife? Or sorry. Just you?
stewart_read: Minor self-corrected verbal stumble — rep starts to ask about a spouse, catches himself, and clarifies. Not a substantive failure; the correction happens in the same breath.
coaching_implication: Not worth a coaching beat on its own — flag only if it recurs as a pattern across other calls from this rep.

quote: Is she she looking into solar too?
stewart_read: The customer had just said thirty seconds earlier that Mary Anne 'owns the home' and that the household already has solar installed. Asking whether she's 'looking into solar too' shows the rep isn't tracking facts the customer just gave him — a concrete instance of information not being retained mid-call, distinct from the earlier title-question stumble.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep could have been probing whether Mary Anne independently wants an unrelated NEW solar purchase — but nothing in the transcript supports this; the more direct reading is a fact-tracking miss.
coaching_implication: This is the sharper example to replay with the rep: two customer statements were given (co-owner, already has solar) and the very next rep question ignores both. Coach on active-listening / note-taking during verify so stated facts don't get re-asked.

quote: Are you looking at details for new panels? I'm I'm not looking to buy any more panels. I just need the removal and reinstallation.
stewart_read: This is the first explicit signal that the customer's need doesn't fit the standard new-install script. Removal/reinstall for a home renovation is a scenario the schema flags as requiring recognition and routing (e.g., supervisor consult or a different track), not continued new-install qualification.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have believed that building a 'design' is a necessary universal first step regardless of scenario type, making this a knowledge gap about process rather than a refusal to adapt.
coaching_implication: Train reps to recognize removal/reinstall-only requests as a distinct scenario immediately and either get a direct answer ready ('yes, we do offer standalone removal/reinstall') or transparently say 'let me check on that for you' rather than defaulting to the new-install design pitch.

quote: Well so we have a program. It's called the the bill swap. And, we actually remove your power bill, and we replace it with a lower and cheaper solar bill.
stewart_read: Rep pitches the full bill-swap financial mechanism to a customer who has already stated he owns his system outright and isn't buying new panels — this pitch is irrelevant to his actual need and is closer-tier program content delivered prematurely and to the wrong scenario.
alternative_hypothesis: This could be read as an attempt to re-engage a suspicious customer with value framing rather than pure scope creep — and it did work briefly (customer says 'I'm curious to hear more' at 02:53) — but it reinforces the wrong mental model (new purchase) that later causes the breakdown.
coaching_implication: Even though this briefly worked, it set up the very confusion that ended the call — the customer now believes he's being sold new panels. Coach the rep to lead with clarifying the actual service need before pitching any program.

quote: I mean, do do you guys just have the service to remove the panels?
stewart_read: This is a direct, answerable yes/no question from the customer. Instead of a clean answer, the rep again pivots to needing a design and mentions talking to a 'specialist' only in the next exchange. The customer is handing the rep the exact question that would resolve the call.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may not have known the true answer and was stalling honestly rather than deflecting strategically — a knowledge gap rather than a scripted reflex.
coaching_implication: If the rep genuinely doesn't know whether Ion offers standalone removal/reinstall, that's a knowledge gap to close with management. If the rep does know but defaults to script anyway, that's a scope/procedure coaching point about answering direct questions plainly before bridging to next steps.
